newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco firms seek national media campaign on suit.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco firms seek national media campaign on suit.

text.p: Tobacco companies Tuesday demanded a national media campaign to inform potential plaintiffs of a class-action lawsuit brought by flight attendants who claim they were sickened by cigarette smoke on the job.
A lawyer for the plaintiffs called such a campaign "overkill to the Nth degree" and described it as a tactic to make the lawsuit prohibitively expensive for the flight attendants.

Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye deferred a decision on the demand, which if granted would present a costly hurdle for plaintiffs in a secondhand-smoke lawsuit known as Broin versus Philip Morris.

The lawsuit, filed in 1991, was brought on behalf of 23 non-smoking flight attendants and two survivors of deceased flight attendants. It claims the plaintiffs contracted various medical disorders from breathing smoke in airplane cabins.
Named as defendants were Philip Morris Cos Inc, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holding Corp. and other major tobacco producers.
The case was ruled a class action and the two sides have determined there could be 200,000-300,000 possible members of the class who must be notified that they can join the lawsuit.

At a court hearing Tuesday, plaintiffs' attorney Stanley Rosenblatt presented a notification plan in which up to 200,000 current and former flight attendants whose names could be readily obtained through airline, union and retiree organization records would receive notification letters.
Rosenblatt said others would learn of the lawsuit through published notices in airline, union and retiree publications, media coverage and word-of-mouth.
Attorney Hugh Whiting, representing R.J. Reynolds, said a national campaign -- with paid ads in newspapers and magazines -- would be needed in addition to individual notification.
"I submit that publicity and word of mouth are not a substitute for legal notice," he told the court. "A program of published notice in national media is required."
Rosenblatt called a national media campaign, which could cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, "wasteful."
"That is a tactic and a device simply meant to make it prohibitive and unnecessarily expensive to the plaintiffs," he said.
Kaye, who has heard hours of argument on the notification plan, did not rule. Another hearing was set for Friday, at which he could rule on notification and also set a trial date.
